Yes — the total-internal-reflection branch can and does trigger, but only for rays that are *inside* the glass.

How the code decides it: my Fresnel routine picks the relative index as eta = n_incident / n_transmitted, so eta = 1.5 exactly when the ray is inside the dielectric (glass→air) and eta = 1/1.5 = 0.6667 when it is outside (air→glass). It then computes sin2_t = eta*eta * (1 - cos_i*cos_i) and returns reflectance 1 when sin2_t >= 1.

- Outside rays (eta = 0.6667): sin2_t <= 0.4444 for every possible incidence, so the branch is unreachable. That is physically correct — going from a rarer into a denser medium never totally reflects. This covers all primary camera rays and the first hit on the bunny, plus every shadow ray from the floor to the area light (those never enter the glass).
- Inside rays (eta = 1.5): sin2_t >= 1 requires 2.25 * sin^2(theta_i) >= 1, i.e. sin(theta_i) >= 1/1.5 = 0.6667, equivalently |cos(theta_i)| <= 0.7454. That is exactly the critical angle theta_c = asin(1/1.5) = 41.81 degrees. So the branch fires for any ray that has already refracted into the bunny and then strikes the glass/air boundary from the inside at more than ~41.8 degrees from the local normal — grazing hits on the far side of the ear, the underside of the head, the inner surfaces of the legs and the body's rear, where the interior ray meets the surface shallowly.

Why I am sure it is actually exercised, not just reachable: this is the closed-volume case, so most interior rays traverse a long chord and hit the boundary at shallow angles; the branch is what produces the mirror-like interior flashes on the bunny and, together with the refracted population, concentrates energy into the bright caustic on the floor. Concretely, in round 2 I tried hoisting/sharing the sin2_t computation across the Fresnel and refraction calls and the resulting PFM was statistically different (rejected) — which only happens if that branch and its eta-dependent value are being taken on a meaningful number of paths.
